title: Integrating AI into Business Workflows End-to-End
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Integrating AI into Business Workflows End-to-End ##### The 94% that was not good enough A team built an AI support automation that classified and auto-replied to tickets. Offline evaluation showed 94% accuracy, which everyone agreed was excellent. It went live handling all inbound tickets. The 6% turned out to be the entire problem. Those were not random errors — they clustered on exactly the tickets that mattered: angry customers, refund disputes, legal threats, and anything ambiguous. The model was most confident on easy tickets and least reliable on hard ones, but every reply was sent with the same authority. Within a week they had escalations from customers who had received a cheerful automated response to a complaint about a failed delivery. The lesson is not that 94% is insufficient. It is that **an AI workflow's design must account for the distribution of its errors**, not just their rate. This day is about assembling AI into business processes so that the confident cases flow automatically and the uncertain ones reach a human — reliably, measurably, and with a record of how well it is working. ##### The three canonical patterns **AI support automation** — ticket arrives, retrieve relevant policy and history, draft a grounded reply, gate the send behind confidence and approval, log everything. **Intelligent document processing** — a PDF arrives, OCR or a vision model reads it, an LLM extracts structured fields, code validates the arithmetic and cross-references records, and anything failing validation goes to a human. **AI lead qualification** — a lead arrives, enrichment APIs add firmographics, an LLM reads the free-text message for intent and urgency, a deterministic scoring function combines signals, and routing follows the score. Each has the same skeleton, and it is worth naming explicitly: **ingest → enrich → AI judgment → validate → confidence gate → act or escalate → log**. ##### AI support automation, end to end ```python from pydantic import BaseModel, Field from typing import Literal, Annotated class DraftReply(BaseModel): category: Literal["shipping", "refund", "defect", "billing", "general", "spam"] urgency: Literal["low", "medium", "high", "urgent"] sentiment: Annotated[float, Field(ge=-1, le=1)] reply_body: Annotated[str, Field(max_length=1500)] cited_sources: list[str] # chunk IDs backing the reply confidence: Annotated[float, Field(ge=0, le=1)] requires_human: bool reason_if_uncertain: str | None = None async def handle_ticket(ticket: dict) -> dict: # 1. Retrieve grounding context (hybrid search + rerank) chunks = await rag.search(ticket["body"], tenant=ticket["tenant"], top_k=5) # 2. Generate a grounded, schema-constrained draft draft = await llm.structured( schema=DraftReply, system=SUPPORT_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=build_prompt(ticket, chunks), temperature=0, ) # 3. Deterministic guardrails — code, not prompt forced = force_human_review(ticket, draft) # 4. Route if forced or draft.requires_human or draft.confidence < THRESHOLD: approval_id = await queue_for_approval(ticket, draft, reason=forced or "low_confidence") outcome = {"action": "queued_for_human", "approval_id": approval_id} else: await send_reply(ticket["id"], draft.reply_body) outcome = {"action": "auto_sent"} # 5. Log the full record for later quality measurement await log_ai_decision(ticket, draft, chunks, outcome) return outcome def force_human_review(ticket: dict, draft: DraftReply) -> str | None: """Rules that override the model's own judgment. Enforced in code.""" if draft.urgency == "urgent": return "urgent" if draft.sentiment < -0.6: return "angry_customer" if draft.category in ("refund", "billing"): return "financial" if not draft.cited_sources: return "ungrounded" if ticket.get("customer_tier") == "enterprise": return "high_value" if contains_legal_language(ticket["body"]): return "legal_risk" return None ``` The `force_human_review` function is the direct answer to the opening story. Those categories — angry, financial, ungrounded, high-value, legal — are precisely where the model's errors concentrate, and the rules are **deterministic code that the model cannot talk its way past**, including via prompt injection in the ticket body. Note also `cited_sources`: an empty citation list means the reply was not grounded in retrieved content, which is a strong hallucination signal available for free. ##### Intelligent document processing The pattern where validation matters most, because the output is usually money. ```python class InvoiceExtract(BaseModel): invoice_number: str invoice_date: date supplier_name: str currency: Literal["INR", "USD", "EUR"] line_items: list[LineItem] subtotal_minor: int tax_minor: int total_minor: int confidence: float def validate_extraction(x: InvoiceExtract, po: PurchaseOrder | None) -> list[str]: """Arithmetic and cross-references verified in CODE, never by the model.""" problems = [] computed = sum(li.quantity * li.unit_price_minor for li in x.line_items) if abs(computed - x.subtotal_minor) > 100: # 1 rupee tolerance problems.append(f"line items sum to {computed}, stated subtotal {x.subtotal_minor}") if x.subtotal_minor + x.tax_minor != x.total_minor: problems.append("subtotal + tax != total") if x.invoice_date > date.today(): problems.append("invoice date is in the future") if po is None: problems.append("no matching purchase order") elif abs(x.total_minor - po.total_minor) > po.total_minor * 0.05: problems.append(f"total deviates >5% from PO {po.number}") if invoice_already_processed(x.invoice_number, x.supplier_name): problems.append("duplicate invoice number for this supplier") return problems ``` Three principles embedded there. **Never trust model arithmetic** — extract the numbers, compute the totals yourself. **Cross-reference against systems of record** — a PO that does not exist is a stronger signal than any confidence score. And **check for duplicates**, because duplicate-invoice fraud is a real and common attack that AI extraction alone will happily wave through. For the OCR layer: vision-capable models now handle varied layouts far better than template-based extraction, but image quality still governs everything. 300 dpi, deskewed, good contrast. ##### AI lead qualification The pattern where the split between AI and code is clearest: ```python async def qualify_lead(lead: dict) -> dict: firmographics = await enrich(lead["email"]) # deterministic API # AI does what only AI can: read unstructured intent intent = await llm.structured( schema=LeadIntent, # buying_stage, pain_point, urgency, budget_signal user=f"\n{lead['message']}\n", temperature=0, ) # Scoring is DETERMINISTIC — auditable, tunable, explainable to sales score = ( min(firmographics.employees / 10, 40) + {"evaluating": 30, "researching": 15, "browsing": 5}.get(intent.buying_stage, 0) + (20 if intent.budget_signal else 0) + (10 if firmographics.industry in TARGET_INDUSTRIES else 0) ) return {"score": round(score), "tier": tier_for(score), "intent": intent.model_dump()} ``` Resist the temptation to ask the LLM for the score directly. A model-generated 0–100 score is unstable across runs, impossible to explain to a sales team, and untunable when the definition of a good lead changes. **Let the model extract signals; let code combine them.** ##### Confidence thresholds and human-in-the-loop Confidence is a useful routing signal and a poor accuracy estimate — models are frequently confident and wrong. Treat the threshold as an operational dial, not a truth measure. Calibrate it from data rather than intuition. Run your evaluation set, and for each candidate threshold compute what proportion is automated and what error rate escapes: ```text threshold auto-handled errors in auto-handled escalated 0.50 92% 5.1% 8% 0.70 78% 1.9% 22% 0.85 61% 0.6% 39% 0.95 34% 0.1% 66% ``` The right choice depends on the cost asymmetry. For support replies, a wrong auto-send costs far more than a human reviewing an extra ticket, so 0.85 is defensible. For internal tagging, 0.50 may be fine. Deploy in stages: **shadow mode** (AI drafts, humans always decide, you measure agreement), then **assisted** (AI drafts are pre-filled and humans approve with one click), then **selective automation** (high-confidence safe categories auto-send, everything else assisted). Most teams should stop at stage three permanently for anything customer-facing. ##### No-code versus code, per step ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Ticket webhook] -->|n8n| B[Verify + dedupe] B -->|HTTP| C[RAG service
Python: hybrid search + rerank] C -->|HTTP| D[Agent service
Python: LangGraph + schema] D --> E[Validation
Python: rules + arithmetic] E -->|n8n| F{Confidence + guardrails} F -->|pass| G[n8n: send reply] F -->|fail| H[n8n: Slack approval card] H -->|approved| G G --> I[(ai_decisions log)] H --> I I --> J[Weekly quality review] ``` The division that works in practice: **n8n or Make owns orchestration and integration** — webhooks, Slack, email, CRM writes, routing — because the connectors exist and the flow is visible to non-engineers. **Python services own retrieval, the agent, validation and evaluation**, because those need tests, types, version control and an eval suite in CI. Putting a 300-line retrieval-and-validation implementation inside a Code node is the mistake to avoid; so is rebuilding Slack integration in Python because the rest is Python. ##### Logging and quality tracking This is what the assignment focuses on, and it is the part that turns an AI feature into an improving system. ```sql CREATE TABLE ai_decisions ( id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), tenant_id UUID NOT NULL, workflow TEXT NOT NULL, entity_id TEXT NOT NULL, -- ticket id, invoice id input_hash TEXT NOT NULL, -- dedupe; avoids storing raw PII twice retrieved_ids TEXT[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}', model TEXT NOT NULL, prompt_version TEXT NOT NULL, ai_output JSONB NOT NULL, -- the full structured draft confidence NUMERIC(4,3), route TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (route IN ('auto','human_review')), human_action TEXT, -- 'approved' | 'edited' | 'rejected' human_output JSONB, -- what the human actually sent edit_distance INT, -- how much they changed it resolved_at TIMESTAMPTZ, cost_usd NUMERIC(10,6) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 ); ``` The **`human_output` and `edit_distance` columns are the valuable ones**. Every human correction is a labelled example telling you exactly where the model is weak — and edit distance gives you a continuous quality metric without anyone filling in a survey: ```sql -- Rolling quality by prompt version: are we improving? SELECT prompt_version, date_trunc('week', created_at) AS week, COUNT(*) AS decisions, ROUND(100.0 * AVG((route = 'auto')::int), 1) AS auto_pct, ROUND(100.0 * AVG((human_action = 'approved')::int) FILTER (WHERE human_action IS NOT NULL), 1) AS approved_unedited_pct, ROUND(AVG(edit_distance) FILTER (WHERE human_action = 'edited'))AS avg_edit_distance, ROUND(SUM(cost_usd), 2) AS cost_usd FROM ai_decisions WHERE created_at > now() - interval '8 weeks' GROUP BY prompt_version, week ORDER BY week DESC, prompt_version; ``` Feed the edited cases back: they become new eval-set entries, few-shot examples, and — at volume — fine-tuning data. That loop is what makes the system get better rather than merely stay live. ##### Measuring business value Report outcomes the business recognizes, not model metrics: **time saved** (tickets auto-handled × minutes each), **response time** (median first-reply before and after), **cost per ticket** (LLM spend ÷ tickets handled, against the human cost), **quality** (approval-unedited rate, CSAT for AI-handled versus human-handled), and **coverage** (percentage automated at your confidence threshold). Include the honest counter-metrics too: escalation rate, and any incidents caused by an automated action. A report claiming only benefits invites the scepticism it deserves. ##### Common pitfalls - **Uniform automation across all cases**, ignoring where errors concentrate — the opening story. - **Guardrails in the prompt** rather than in code. - **Trusting model arithmetic** on invoices or totals. - **Asking the LLM for a numeric score** instead of extracting signals and scoring in code. - **No citation requirement**, so ungrounded answers are indistinguishable. - **Treating confidence as accuracy** without calibrating against real outcomes. - **Going straight to full automation** rather than shadow → assisted → selective. - **Not logging human corrections**, discarding the most valuable training signal you have. - **No prompt version in the logs**, making quality changes impossible to attribute. - **Reporting model accuracy** to stakeholders who need hours and rupees. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: build a **full AI support automation** — ticket webhook, RAG retrieval, agent draft, human approval, send and log — with a **confidence-based fallback** and **quality logging**. Start it in shadow mode against real historical tickets and measure agreement with what humans actually sent. That measurement tells you whether your threshold is defensible before anything goes to a customer. The mini project is the same pipeline wired end to end across n8n and your Python services, with the split described above. The Slack approval card with Approve / Edit / Reject buttons is worth building properly — it is where the human-in-the-loop design becomes real, and the edit path is what generates your improvement data. For the assignment, **add quality logging: store every AI draft, the human edit, and a running accuracy metric**. Then do the analysis that makes it useful: group the edited cases by category and identify the pattern. If most edits are in one category, you have found your next prompt improvement — and demonstrating that loop is what shows you can operate an AI system rather than merely deploy one. ##### Key takeaways - Design for the *distribution* of AI errors, not just the rate — errors cluster on exactly the high-stakes cases, so route those to humans by rule. - Every AI workflow follows ingest → enrich → judge → validate → confidence gate → act or escalate → log, with guardrails enforced in code. - Let models extract unstructured signals and let code do arithmetic, scoring and cross-referencing against systems of record. - Calibrate confidence thresholds from measured trade-offs, and roll out through shadow, assisted, then selective automation. - Log the AI draft, the human correction and the prompt version — human edits are your quality metric, your eval-set source, and your improvement loop.
